projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Schneider was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, William E. Schneider. Mr. Schneider served in the US Army. He served in the Pacific Theater and his highest rank was T/3. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Schneider's home in [address redacted], on October 23rd, 2002. William was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And where were you living when World War II started for America?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: When the, when the war started for America I was living in Los Angeles, California, at which time I was employed by Douglas Aircraft. We were building, we were building war aircraft for the, this was before the war, this was for the war effort. And I specialized working on the, on the A-20, which was a bomber for the American Air Corps and the DB-7, which was the same version for the British Air Corps. From that time, from that time, I enlisted in the Army and the first time I went down to be enlisted I got turned down because of my eyesight, but I wasn't going to let that stop me and I tried, a little bit later I went down again and I enlisted again and I passed the eye test. I don't know if I really did or not, but, but they took me this time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were living in Los Angeles when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yes, I was, I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yes, I do remember that day. That particular day I was at a movie in Los Angeles. We had gone to a movie and in the middle of the movie, they stopped the movie and a man come out on the stage and he said we want everyone to listen, any enlisted men in the audience are to report immediately to their base camp. And at that time they didn't tell us that Pearl Harbor had been attacked, it was after we got out of the movie that we really found out. But at this time I was, I was still with Douglas. I hadn't enlisted yet. It was shortly after this that I had enlisted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now was Los Angeles a scary place to be in those first days?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yes, Los Angeles was a scary place because, I tell you why, being a coast city we had to turn all of our lights out. No one was allowed to have any lights, even the headlights on the cars and you had to keep your shades pulled. And they finally came out with the cars that we put reflectors or deflectors on our headlights so that the cars could not be seen from the air.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be just a little hood over the top there?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yeah, it was like a hood. It was like a blue hood that went over the top of the headlight and made the lights very dim and hard, they weren't white lights like we're normal to seeing, and they were real dull lights, but that was to keep the enemy, or whatever, from designated, the hot spots. And I might say, too, that they camouflaged the plant where I was working. I was working in Santa Monica at the time, which was Douglas Aircraft base, and they camouflaged this base so well that you could never tell there was an air plant, and airplane manufacturing plant underneath us. They completely built a platform over and above it. Planted grass there and had cows grazing in the meadow and rows, everything like that, and no one could have ever, would ever know that there was a defense plant underneath it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had cows grazing on the roof, basically?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Right, we, actually we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: And of course, we worked there, besides building the bomber planes there, we were also making the DC-3s and the DC-4s which were used for transport and later went in, were used in the Army, used for the transfer of trap -- for troops and paratroopers. But it was, oh, it was shortly after this that when I enlisted in the Army, I went downtown to Los Angeles and enlisted. And this was, oh, this was in late 1943, I had to get old enough besides being able to see, but I enlisted in San Pedro, California, which is a, is a suburb of Los Angeles, right on the water. And after my enlisted -- enlistment they sent us home for a weekend, issued us clothes and everything, but one of the experiences after I had enlisted was they had to keep us busy, so they kept us digging ditches and filling other ditches with the ditches we dug. And one day they asked for volunteer truck drivers. Well, a lot of guys figured, well, this going to be an easy way out so, they all volunteered to be the volunteer truck drivers, and when they picked them out of the line-up, they give each one of them a wheelbarrow and that was their truck. But, after we had, after we had received our issue of clothes and give you some orientation of how to make a bed and all of this type of stuff, we were put on the train, troop train, and we were sent to Aberdeen, Maryland. But I'll never forget the train had to make a change in Brownsville, Texas, and we were allowed to get off of the train. They said it would be about a forty-five minute stop over. So we got off the train. When we come back the train was gone. And we were just scared to death. Here we are, been in the Army a week and we're AWOL already. But we were able to find out that they had just moved the train over to seven or eight tracks from where the train stopped and there we went, from there on we went to Aberdeen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training then?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, Aberdeen, Aberdeen, Maryland, was a training base for equipment for tanks, heavy tanks, high speed tractors, artillery, this type of thing. And we were put, first of all we were put in a battalion, where we received our basic training. And during the basic training, one of the requirements was you had to go to the rifle range and you had to pass the rifle range with the, with the, with the Springfield '03 rifle and just before we went to the range I come down with pneumonia. Well, they put me in the hospital and if you missed the -- or missed being at the rifle range, you had to start your basic training all over. So I talked the doctor into letting me out of the hospital and going to the range and fire for score on the range and I was the highest bat in the battalion in the score when it was all over with. But we received our training in Atlanta. We lived in, we lived in tar paper shacks. They were long tar paper shacks and they had, each one had a pot belly stove in it. And of course, it was, each day you were put out on the site, whether it was KP or take care of the stoves or whatever, but we had to, at nighttime when it was cold, and it was cold in Aberdeen in the winter time, and had to keep the fire going for the rest of the troops. And they changed, about three times during the night they changed, but we got our, we got our basic training in Aberdeen. And after the basic training, after we went through all of that, then we went, what they called the Ordinance School. The Ordinance School was kind of like graduating from high school, like going into college so far as ordinance was concerned. And I was assigned to a tractor division, which was a, they called in the Army, it was a high speed tractor, which was used for pulling the 105 guns. And I was assigned to an automotive division at the same time. And here we got, you might say, the basic training in that. After the graduation from that, we were sent, we were all, our battalion was called together and we were all issued ODs. We figured, well, we're issued these ODs, something is coming up. So it did come up and we were sent to Shenango, which is Sharon, Pennsylvania. And at Shenango, I and several of the other, the trooper base supplement people in case someone else got sick or something, couldn't go, why, we went in their place. Well, as it was, everybody was there, so I went back to my barracks at which time I and a group of men were shipped down to the Atlanta Ordinance Depot. At the Atlanta Ordinance Depot we went into a higher tech training on the high speed tanks and tractors and so on and so forth. We spent a great deal of time there and we thought, well, we're ready to go now, so we were assigned and getting ready for another ship. We figured, well, this is it. We wound up in Texarkana, Texas, which was the, which was the Texarkana Ordinance Base, Red River Valley it was called. We got additional training there. And our training encompassed not only training on the, on the artillery and on the machines, it also consisted of a training program where we were taught to train other people the same things that we had learned in our past experience. Well, come along, oh, this was probably several weeks before Easter we got our shipping orders again. We were shipped to, back to Los Angeles, across country again, from east to west. Wound up in Los Angeles where we boarded a train and went up to Pittsburg, California. Pittsburg, California is a, is a suburb of San Francisco and the camp there was Stoneman. Well, we figured now, this is, this is really it, because when we got there, here were the troop ships and all were waiting for us, and we went from, we went from there. We all were given a birth in the ship. It was the Cape Mendocino. It was an English ship, it was a freighter, and there were four hundred in our battalion and we were assigned a bunk, each was assigned a bunk. Well, the bunks were in the ship and the bunks were like hammocks and they were six stories or six bunks high. And we didn't find out until about a little while after that that our bunks were twenty foot under the sea level. If we had gotten a torpedo or anything, we would have been, would have been covered with water. But anyway, during this, during this trip over, which by the way took thirty-two days, we had to, had to, we had, they called it STAT 2 and C. STAT 2 was the morning just before sunrise. And I was assigned a lifeboat on the ship and I was responsible if there should be an attack in the morning, or whenever there would be an attack I was assigned to see the lifeboat was properly fitted with people and lowered into the water, which never happened. But it was really a mess about five or six days after we left we went under the Golden Gate Bridge and after we left we began to get what is commonly known as seasickness. And there was hardly anybody that was below deck. They were just sick. They couldn't eat. They couldn't -- that -- Fortunately I wasn't one of them. But about the end of the seventh or eighth day, things started to get better. Well, we found out that besides our four hundred on this freighter, on the Cape Mendocino, were sixteen hundred other troops from another division. So we had our meals, breakfast, lunch and dinner, they called it, and we went down into the galley by number. They called you Charley Four, Charley Three, whatever your group number was was your turn to eat. And it seemed like you had no more finished your breakfast or your lunch or whatever it was, that they are calling Charley Four again, because it took that long to go through the line to get up to the next meal. But it was so hot and we're now, we now traveling down in the south seas and it was so hot that you couldn't really bear to stay in the galley. It was over a hundred degrees. And besides, as the ship swayed from side to side, your tray slid back and forth on the, on your table, which you had to stand up to eat and your tray slid back and forth. I'm not sure that we ate, ate on our whole meal off of the same tray or not. But anyway, we got over that and we finally come, we crossed the equator. We had the big, we had the big party for the equator, for King Neptune, and the officers were mainly just prey. And they would bring charges against these officers and the officers would, had better deny, and of course, if you denied, it just made it twice as bad for you, and they had to do such things as eat raw eggs and they squirted them with a fire hose and they made them undress and put diapers on them and all, and we finally got that ritual over. By this time we're approaching Australia. Well, as we approach it the ship made a big circle and we approached Australia. We got the offers that we were to go to Pulo. Pulo was an island north of Australia and we said well, you know, we didn't really know where we were going, but when we got to Pulo, which was maybe six, seven, eight days later, we met with a convoy of ships. And this convoy of ships went up through the islands of the Phil -- (tape skips) -- destination was Manila. Well, when we got to Manila we pulled in the bay and we were utterly surprised as we pulled in the bay. There wasn't really hardly room for us because out of the bay, sticking up from out of the water were a hundred and one masts of ships that were sunk and sitting in the bottom of the bay. But at any rate, we finally did get a dockage and we proceeded to be given assignments for unloading the ships and setting up a camp in Manila. Well, it seemed like the next day, one of the officers had to go into the City of Manila on some official business and I was appointed his escort or his guard. But they sent us, we had carbines, we were in ordinance, so we had carbines, and they sent me along to guard him with blank ammunition. Well, that was kind of a mistake, but that was soon corrected, because when the fellows were put on guard duty they also had blank ammunition, and when the Japs started coming from under the lily pads in the Pasig River they had no defense. So we got that straightened out. Our main assignment in Manila was to build an ordinance depot for the repair of all the ordinance, of the tanks and the tractors and the cars and the artillery. And we were given Filipino laborers as helpers to build this camp. But in the meantime a certain number of them were also assigned to this Japanese graveyard where there were -- it wasn't really a graveyard because the Japs weren't, they weren't really buried, they were just laying all around. We had to clear that up and we set up six-man tents. And these six-man tents we set up in the air, four foot off of the ground, because of the monsoons and the water. But anyway, we got this done, got it set up and built the latrines and got a kitchen set up and all, and one of the obstacles there was in the mess kitchen, was during the night, the Japs would couple down Pasig River and they were floating under lily leaves, and the lily leaves, oh, they were big, they were maybe three or four foot, and these Japs would come under the lily leaves and then get their chance to sneak up into our kitchen and steal our food. So we finally got that straightened out. But then we really got down to business after that and we were not, we were what you would, we weren't on the front lines, we were in a combat zone, but our job was to retrieve tanks and high speed tractors, whatever, was to retrieve it, bring them to the shops and repair them. At the same time it was our job to take these Filipino laborers and teach them what we were doing on the repair of these items. So we set that up and got that set up where we had them trained. One kind of funny thing there we had the Water Buffaloes, which were amphibious tanks just down the river where we were stationed and in Manila was a big beer factory, or whatever you might want to call it, but this was never touched because they had an agreement. There was an agreement with the Japanese and the Americans, everybody, that that beer factory should not be touched. So every once in a while we'd kind of have to try out one of our repairs, we'd float down the Pasig River and stop at the beer factory and have a little treat of some cold beer. It was the coldest beer I think I have ever had in my life. But anyway, this went on and then we got, we got the notification that -- Well, prior to this, really I might mention, while we were at sea, we got, we got the notification by radio on the ship that President Roosevelt had passed away. And of course, radio communication on ship was, was not allowed, but in this particular case they did break radio silence to make this announcement. But anyway, we went through and repaired these tanks. Later on they could kind of see the beginning of the end, we were assigned the assignment of all of these tractors and tanks and guns and everything we had, we had a place on the island which was like a great big flat storage field and our job was to activate all of these machines that were coming in by ship, we were to activate them, get them running, and then we would drive them out, we would drive them out and we would park them in this great big parking space where there is thousands and thousands and thousands of them. We kind of, we kind of got a kick out of that job in a way, because the Filipinos didn't really like us too well and we kind of liked them less because they used to come steal everything out of our tents and stuff. So, on the way driving these tanks out to the storage place we'd go down these streets and had big bomb holes in them and they were full of water. So we kind of got a kick out of finding the biggest bottom -- bomb hole full of water and it was our, it was our desire to hit that to see how much we could splash the Filipinos as we went by. But it was shortly after this I was injured and I was sent to the hospital there and I was in the hospital probably three or four weeks and I was notified that my injury was, I would not get well soon enough that I would be of any asset, actually, to the war at that time. And I was put on a ship, USS Hospital Ship Marigold, and we were shipped back to the States. And ironically, on our way back we come up and we were just, as we made our arch out of the Philippines coming back to San Francisco, we were just a few miles off the Aleutian Islands and as we made the arch to come down to San Francisco, we could all see the Aleutian Islands. By this time the war was over and I went on to the hospital in Riverside, California, and from there transferred to Fitzsimons General Hospital in Denver, Colorado. Had surgery and had repairs made, and in February, 1946, I was given my honorable discharge and sent back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you mention how you were hurt?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yes, we were working on a high speed tractor and the shrapnel or steel from the tractor, I got hit in both hands and made, my hands were, I couldn't really use my hands and lost a finger and a few things. But it was nothing compared to what some of the boys over there got. But things worked out. I got out of the Army in February, came home, my home was actually in South Dakota, came home to South Dakota and then spent some time there and then shortly come to Cleveland and got married to the girl that I met while I was down in Atlanta during the war. So, in March, 1946, we were married and that was the beginning of our civilian life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So I assumed you wrote letters back and forth?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Oh, my gosh, I have trunks full of letters. They are full of holes. They look, some of the letters I wrote looked like a colander where they had, where they had audited the letter and cut out things that they didn't want to know. The funny thing, I wanted to let my folks know where I was at and in my hometown in Tyndall, South Dakota, we had a family there by the name of Henderson. And one of the boys in the family had only one leg. And he lived in Springfield, South Dakota. So I was able to tell my folks where I was because Henderson field was near Manila, so I told them, I was asking them how is that Henderson boy from Springfield getting along. And that was kind of the clue to let them know where I was at the time. But since that time, we have had our ups and downs, but we were married and we have two lovely boys now and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would she write to you?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, she would write me about the movies she had been to and about the -- Oh, what do I want to say? -- the USO, different things there. And they had kind of little clubs there that they did to help the war effort and all of that kind of thing. I think she behaved herself while I was gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much entertainment when you were over there, overseas?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Not, not very much, occasionally. I could recall one time where they got all the, all the gang together, all the troops that were all in the vicinity, took us to this great big area and they put on the play South Pacific. And we all, that was one of the entertainments we got. Other than that, we didn't have much there but the Salvation Army and Red Cross, which was a cup of coffee maybe or something like that. That was pretty much it. Later, later during the period over there we were able to put a ball field together and we formed baseball clubs over there in our spare time, if we had any spare time, and had baseball clubs. And I forget who one of the ball players was. He was from the Cleveland Indians though, and it was Early Wynn or somebody, but he was in, he was in our ball club at the same time. But that was about the extent of the entertainment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now you said you were, as you were heading to Manila, you heard the news about FDR. What was your reaction to the news?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, it kind of scared me, because I says here we are at war without a leader. But of course, immediately, Harry Truman was put in. And well, Harry Truman, too, was really kind of nobody that we knew. We didn't -- Who was Harry Truman? But he stepped in. He did his job and did it to the satisfaction I believe of everyone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you would have probably arrived in Manila somewhere around April of '45, is that right?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: It was, it was right after, after the death of President Roosevelt. It seems to me it was right after Easter time that year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was about the same time, right.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So specifically what was your job?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: My job was specifically when we got the headquarters set together was to supervise the Filipinos on the repair. And we were, at this particular time, my group was working on the high speed tractor, which pulled the 105 millimeter cannons. They were big things. They were big, they were big machines, had two engines to each one. Waukesha had big engines, you know, and it was tracked like a tank, but had no protection over the top of them like a tank. You had a canvas top on it, and the reason for the canvas top was that soldiers liked, if they were attacked, they liked to get underneath a turret or steel top, which was no protection. So they started putting canvas tops on them because they knew, everyone knew that a canvas top wasn't going to stop any ordinance from coming in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your rank?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: I was a T/3, a Tech Sergeant, started out. Worked our way up from Private to T/3 and I was discharged with a T/3.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now you mentioned a few problems with the Filipinos. Did you get along with them, mainly?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, I had a friend over there. I had met, I had met, some young children used to come by the fence by our headquarters and we got to know them. And I remember I called one of them "Bright Eyes" and they had a tar paper shack not far from our camp and we got to know them, and we would give them "choc-late" as they called it and candy bars and that. So, one night, my buddy, Sal, and myself were invited to their place. They want to be good to the American soldier. We were invited over there for dinner or lunch or whatever. And when they served it, they served us chicken with all the feathers on it. Well, the way they prepared their chicken over there, they took the chicken and they wrapped it in wet papers or something and baked it and then when you pulled the paper off, the feathers and all come off. And I didn't do too well that night. My buddy, he ate some of it, but that was about the extent of mine. But the Filipinos used to come and they used to steal from us. They'd come at nighttime and they'd reach up, as I told you our cots were four foot above, they'd reach up over the top and they would pull the stuff out of our foot lockers. And sometimes you'd wake up in the morning and we didn't have any clothes to put on. And yet we all slept with a, we called it a "grease gun," which was a submachine gun. We all slept with one under our pillow, but they were so quiet that you didn't even, we didn't know they were there and that kind of turned us against them. But some of the -- We used to pull tricks on them, too. I can remember we used to get our cigarette rations, it would be our carton of cigarettes. They would come in a carton but they were wrapped in wax paper. So after they pulled a few tricks on them, we pulled a few on them and we would take the cigarettes out and fill the carton up with sawdust and sell it back to them for fifteen centavos or whatever it was. But they say Joe, you no good, Joe, you no good. The language over there was, they called it Tagalog and we kind of get to, we got to learn a little bit of the Tagalog. I can remember bewalang tagasant (phonetic) meant beware, stay away. Or maganda delaga (phonetic), that meant a beautiful girl, and buna was banana, pina was pineapple. Different stuff like that. But they pretty much, the Filipino population there was, I am going to say probably half Spanish people. And the Spanish people we got along pretty well with them, but they pretty much all talked and understood English. You didn't hear much of the Tagalog over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there Japanese there the whole time then right up until the end of the war?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Oh, yes. We had, in Manila, they have a place called the "Walled City." And this Walled City which was a big fort compound that was built right in the center of the City of Manila with big walls around it. And up until the time, and even after the time the war was over, we still had Japanese hidden out in the Walled City and the snipers, and the other place that the Japs would go, it was against policy over there, it was kind of an unwritten law, you don't destroy the churches, which was mostly was Catholic religion over there, but what had happened, the Japanese got in all of these churches and set their fortresses up in the churches, because they were aware that they weren't going to be attacked being in a church. However, after a while, it didn't really make any difference if it was a church or not. And the Japanese, well, even after, even after I left Manila, I heard of cases of the Japanese in the hills and the mountains there were still couldn't believe that the war was over and were still taking pot shots at our people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies that you had over there?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Memories of buddies?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yes, I had, of course, now we have lost contact, but there was a group of maybe five or six of them, we kind of formed together and everything we did we kind of stayed as a group. And after, after the war we lost contact. I started to tell you before about the little girl that we called Bright Eyes, after that dinner we had with them we made friends with the family and for quite some time after I got back to the States we corresponded. He was a banker in a bank in Manila and we used to write letters back and forth and he would tell us how things were happening over there and I would write him and give him all the information here and then eventually we lost contact.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were on your way back when the bombs were dropped? Was that the way that happened, the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: No, that was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still in the Philippines?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: -- just a short time, the atomic bombs happened a short time before I came back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Because after I was injured over there I was in the hospital for probably oh, probably a month or six weeks. It was during this period of time, but we were on our way back after the bombs, after the bombs were dropped. Of course, when we heard the about the atomic bombs, we, we didn't really know what the atomic bomb even was until afterwards when we got more information.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Could you grasp at all what that was? What were the rumors?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, the rumors, the rumors were that Japan was just literally wiped off the face of the earth, which I guess was pretty accurate. And it was right after that if I recall, it was right after that that the war, the war, they signed the peace agreement and the war was over with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where were you on VJ Day then?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: I was on, aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were aboard ship. Any celebrations on board ship?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, not, not really. We had a rough time coming back. We were on this USS Marigold and coming back up around the Aleutians we run into bad storms. This was in, this was in, like in November, and I can recall the waves hitting the front of the ship and the wave would be completely over the top of the ship to the rear of the ship, the waves were so big, and most everybody was down out of the weather and in their bunks and hanging on for dear life, I guess, but we made it okay. But that was that was a pretty long trip from Manila to San Pedro, California in a pair of pajamas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you first see your family when you got back?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: We got back, we come into Riverside, California and then we were transferred by hospital train to Denver. And I am going to say it was just before Christmas in '45 that I got to see the family. And then I was discharged in the end of February in '46.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that reunion with your family like? Were you there?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: No, not yet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reunion with the family like?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, they were all glad to see me back. Of course, I had a brother who was in the Air Corps and first time my family had been together for years, really, but it was a great occasion. And then I was able, after I got back I was able to get a pass, a week pass or whatever, I come to see her in Cleveland, and then I went back to base and I had another surgery and after I was discharged in March, I come back and we got married. We just have kind of a deal that no marriage during the war. We wanted to be sure that it was over with and that is the way it worked out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Going back to your enlistment, was there any trouble with you enlisting since you were obviously working at a defense-related job?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: No, no, there were no problems at all. They were very happy to get me, but they weren't so fussy the second time around as they were the first time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Which was maybe probably six weeks difference. But it was quite an experience and I am glad I had the experience but I wouldn't want to have it again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, I guess probably the one thing is when one of our, one of our people run over a land mine with this, this D7 Caterpillar tractor and it exploded and killed him. One other one was, kind of a humorous one, one of the guys was, he was on this D7 Caterpillar tractor having his picture taken and he was backing up while they are taking his picture and the tractor, the Caterpillar tractor, backed right into the Pasig River and he darn near drowned in there but we got the tractor out. It destroyed the tractor but that was kind of a humorous occasion, but not too many of them happened either. We had in the city of, in the City of Manila, we had McArthur's headquarters were there in one of the big buildings there. Occasionally, we would go down there, they had like a USO in it besides that, and occasionally we would get down there, but the transportation was, it was kind of a problem unless we had a chance to confiscate a Jeep some place and use it for a day or two till somebody confiscated it from us. It was kind of, the Jeeps were kind of, everybody carried a rotor around in their pocket in case they come across a Jeep they'd be able to start it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because they would remove the rotor when they went inside?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yeah, so we had to have our own.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't have any close encounters with McArthur, you didn't see him up close at all, did you?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: No, no, no. By the time, by that time they had the, they had pretty much moved up north from Manila up in Baguio, in that area up there. We were right, we were right near Bataan, but Bataan was all over with at that time. And we got in kind of, we were kind of got into the late, late part of the war, because I think it was, it was in the spring or the summer of '45 if I'm not mistaken, that Victory in Europe Day came. That was pretty much out of the way, so we just had to deal with the Japanese. And I know there were a lot of troops coming in that were coming in from the European theater, were being transferred to the Pacific theater. But, they never much got to see action other than the ones that had been there all the time. But I have friends, I brought them to the, I brought them to the VFW, the American Legion, and I have friends in there that have some very, very vivid stories to tell, but they don't talk much about it. But luckily I wasn't encountered with anything as bad as that. One guy, one of the fellows out there talks about he was a machine, machine gunner in Okinawa and he says he has down to this, tending to business, and all of a sudden he sees the head fly by with a helmet on it. And of course, we don't really want to talk about them kind of things, but them kind of things happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm sure.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: And it concerns me very much for some of the things that our boys did go through during this war that the generation today doesn't even know about this kind of stuff. They don't really have an inkling. You can ask some of these people who General McArthur were and they will look at you with a stare, not knowing who they were. Or you talk about World War II. Well, sure World War II was fifty-some years ago and some of these youngsters today are only seventeen to eighteen, but you would think, I would think that this would be covered in their history books like they used to do it. But it seems to me, and I could be mistaken, but it seems to me that has kind of taken a back seat to other things. But any veteran, and I would credit to any veteran or any man or woman that spent their time, regardless what they did, they spent their time, they sacrificed their self and says I'll give my life for my country, they deserve the respect. And it upsets me on the days, Memorial Day, the people, instead of coming to a good Memorial Day service to honor our veterans can't wait to get out to the beach or get their picnic going. And the same with, well, I guess I am old fashioned, I call it Armistice Day, but on Vets Day, the same thing. But we have a Vets Day coming up now and for the, oh, for about the last five years or so, our school here has set up a program where every Veterans Day we have a program where our veterans participate in the program. We try to tell the children there, they attend, we try to tell them things that happened during the war, tell them about the flag, tell them about the Pledge of Allegiance and them children sit in that audience and you can hear a pin drop. They just, as attending, and they want to learn this stuff but it's not being taught to them. In fact, I, I have got to get ready for the Veterans Day that is coming up now. That is only a couple, three weeks away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Are you going to speak at a school?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yeah, I do every year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Yeah. I mainly cover the topic of Armistice Day and what it is and why it is. And then we also do the same thing on Memorial Day. We, we, I, when I talk Memorial Day, I talk about the original of Memorial Day, how it was developed, what it means, so on and so forth. It was General Logan's order that the graves be strewn with flowers and at this time it was called Decoration Day. Well, of course, now it's called Memorial Day. A lot of people can't associate Decoration Day and Memorial Day. They don't associate that as one and the same. (End of Side One; Begin Side Two.) Of course, now it has expanded. Now, it's -- You find Memorial Day Celebrations and carnivals and kind of, kind of way down the line something might be mentioned about the veterans. I recall two or three years ago in Seattle, Washington, they used to have a Memorial Day, at this one particular place in Seattle their attendance would be two, three, four thousand people doing the attendance. And about a couple years after that, just recently, as recent as last year, their attendance was only ten or fifteen people. And yet, we're losing our veterans. We're losing our veterans at the rate of fifteen hundred of them a day, which that is a lot of people when you multiply it by the number of days. But, you know, the one thing that really does concern me is that these veterans, and it seems like the American Legion and the VFW are primarily the ones that are tied into this most, but what concerns me really is the younger people and the people coming up, are they going to carry this on, or is it going to gradually fade away and people are just going to forget about it. And I have pictures in the other room of one of the, of one of the Memorials that we celebrated. Get it, Ruth. Get that picture, get the picture that is hanging on the wall in there, the Army picture of Memorial Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After you got out of the hospital, did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after you got out of the Army?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, yes, because after I was released, after I was released from the Army I still had this finger.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: But it was, I couldn't bend it. It was sticking up in the air. So, I had three different operations on this finger to try to save it. And this finger is mainly, it's got hair all around it, it's mainly made out of my arm up here. They took the skin out of my arm and they made my, they made my finger out of it. But other than that, no, I didn't really have any psychological problems after I got out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else comes to mind?

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: No, I, I thing we pretty much covered the main items.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were very well prepared without reading a script.

sp.speaker: William Schneider
sp.p: Well, I guess it kind of comes back to you after you get talking about it, you know. But it was a, it was, like I said, it was a good experience but a terrible experience, too. Whereupon; the interview was concluded.
